title: Recursion, sorting and binary search
summary: Functions that call themselves, what sorting really costs (and JavaScript's sorting trap), and how binary search finds anything in sorted data in a handful of steps.
youWillLearn: How recursion works: a smaller copy of the problem, plus a base case
What the call stack does, and what a stack overflow is
Why sorting costs O(n log n), and why [10, 9, 1].sort() gives the wrong answer
How to write a binary search that does not loop forever or miss by one

glossary.recursion: A function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller piece of the same problem.
glossary.base case: The smallest version of the problem, answered directly without another call. It is what makes recursion stop.
glossary.call stack: The stack where the computer keeps every function call that has started but not finished yet.
glossary.stack overflow: The error you get when the call stack grows past its limit, usually because recursion never reaches its base case.
glossary.comparator: A small function you pass to sort that says which of two items should come first.
glossary.merge sort: A sorting method that splits the list in half, sorts each half the same way, then merges the two sorted halves.
glossary.binary search: Finding a value in sorted data by checking the middle and throwing away the half that cannot contain it, again and again.
glossary.off-by-one: A bug where a loop or index is one step too far or one step short, like stopping at the last item instead of after it.

steps.title: How many loops deep is a folder?
body: Notely wants a note count next to every folder, including everything inside its subfolders. Last lesson you walked the tree with a stack.
But think about writing it with plain loops: one loop per level. Maya's folders could be two levels deep or twelve. You cannot know in advance how many loops to nest.

scene.caption: Folders inside folders, to a depth nobody knows in advance.

steps.title: Recursion: solve a smaller copy
body: Recursion flips the question. A folder's count is its own notes plus the count of each subfolder. And "count of a subfolder" is the same question, one level smaller. So the function calls itself.
It needs a base case: a folder with no subfolders returns its own notes. Without that, it never stops.

callout.text: Russian nesting dolls. To count the dolls, open one and ask the same question about the doll inside. The smallest doll, which does not open, is the base case.

scene.caption: Each folder asks its child the same question. Acme has no children: the base case.

steps.title: The call stack keeps every waiting call
body: Each call waits for its children before it can return. The computer keeps those waiting calls on the call stack, the same last-in, first-out stack from lesson 4.
Acme returns 2 first. Then Clients returns 1 + 2 = 3, Work returns 4 + 3 = 7, and All notes returns 10. Last call in, first call out.

scene.caption: Calls pile up on the way down and finish in reverse order on the way back.

notes.text: Top of the stack finishes first

steps.title: Sorting costs O(n log n)
body: You will rarely write a sort at work. The built-in sort is fast and takes O(n log n), the rung on the Big-O ladder just above O(n). Remember that cost: "sort first" is never free.
But JavaScript has a trap. With no comparator, sort() compares items as text, so 10 comes before 9. It also changes the original array.

code.caption: Negative means a comes first, positive means b comes first.

scene.caption: Same numbers, two results. Without a comparator, JavaScript sorts as text.

steps.title: Merge sort: recursion that sorts
body: Where does n log n come from? Merge sort shows it. Split the list in half, sort each half the same way, then merge the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front item.
A list of one is already sorted: that is the base case. Halving gives about log n levels, and each level merges all n items. Hence O(n log n).

scene.caption: Split down to tiny sorted pieces, then merge back up in order.

steps.title: Binary search: check the middle
body: Now Notely's activity log: millions of events, already sorted by time. Maya asks for everything since 09:00.

Binary search checks the middle event. Before 09:00? The answer is in the right half. At or after? It is in the left half, maybe the middle itself. Each check halves what is left: about 21 checks for two million events. O(log n), but only on sorted data.

callout.text: Guessing a number from 1 to 100 with "higher or lower" hints. Always guess the middle and you never need more than seven guesses.

scene.caption: The middle is at or after 09:00, so everything to its right can be ignored.

steps.title: Finding the first event since 09:00
body: Second check: the middle of what is left is 08:45, before 09:00, so the answer is to its right. Now lo and hi meet at index 2: 09:02 is the first match.
This version is called lower bound. It returns the first index whose value is at or after the target, or the array length if there is none. Learn this one shape and reuse it.

scene.caption: 08:45 is too early, so lo moves past it. lo meets hi at 09:02.

steps.title: Off by one, or not sorted at all
body: Binary search fails in two classic ways. An off-by-one: write lo = mid instead of mid + 1 and the loop can repeat forever. And unsorted input: the search still returns an answer, just a wrong one, with no error.
Recursion fails one way: no reachable base case. The calls pile up until JavaScript throws a stack overflow: RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.

callout.text: When Claude Code writes a binary search, ask: "Where is this array sorted, and by the same key?" Then test it on an empty array, one item, a target before all items and one after all items. For any .sort() on numbers or dates, check that a comparator is passed.

scene.caption: Two events out of order: the search skips 09:05 and confidently returns 09:30.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Recursion solves a smaller copy of the same problem and needs a base case to stop. Calls wait on the call stack.
Sorting costs O(n log n), and in JavaScript needs a comparator for numbers. Binary search finds things in O(log n), but only in sorted data, and only if you get the bounds exactly right.

quiz.question: Claude Code sorts note word counts with counts.sort(). The counts are [120, 45, 9]. What do you get?

options.why: That is what you want, but without a comparator JavaScript compares the values as text.
As text, "120" comes before "45" (1 is before 4), which comes before "9". Pass (a, b) => a - b to sort numbers.

options.text: A TypeError, because sort needs a comparator.
options.why: The comparator is optional, which is exactly why this bug is easy to miss: no error, just a wrong order.

quiz.question: A recursive function that walks Maya's folders crashes with Maximum call stack size exceeded. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Too many notes in one folder.
options.why: Notes in a folder are handled in a loop. They do not add calls to the call stack.

options.text: A folder that contains itself somewhere down the tree, so the base case is never reached.
options.why: A loop in the data means the recursion never hits a folder without children. Calls pile up until the stack overflows.

options.text: Recursion does not work in serverless functions.
options.why: It works anywhere. The call stack limit is the same kind of limit everywhere.

quiz.question: Which situation is the right fit for binary search?

options.text: Finding a note by title in Maya's notes, which are in creation order.
options.why: The list is sorted by date, not by title. Binary search on the wrong key gives wrong answers. A Map by title is simpler.

options.text: Checking whether a tag appears in a list of 12 tags.
options.why: It would work if sorted, but for 12 items a plain scan is simpler and just as fast.

options.text: Finding the first log event after a timestamp in millions of events sorted by time.
options.why: Large, already sorted by the key you search on: about 21 checks for two million events.

takeaways: Recursion = call yourself on a smaller piece + a base case that stops. No reachable base case means a stack overflow.
The built-in sort is O(n log n). For numbers or dates, always pass a comparator: (a, b) => a - b.
sort() changes the array. Use toSorted() when you need a copy.
Binary search is O(log n) on sorted data only. Learn the lower-bound shape: while (lo < hi), lo = mid + 1, hi = mid.
Test searches on empty input, one item, and targets before and after everything.
